content: 1. For patients with extensive tuberculosis (TB) disease or severe forms of extrapulmonary TB, clinical judgment should guide the decision to use longer treatment regimens, as there is insufficient evidence regarding surrogate markers for disease severity or extent. 2. Recent years have seen a growing interest in reducing the duration of treatment for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB). This has led to studies exploring shorter treatment regimens under both programmatic and trial conditions. 3. Based on experiences in various settings, eligible patients can now be treated with a shorter, injectable-sparing regimen lasting 9–12 months. This approach aims to achieve desired treatment outcomes while minimizing the risk of additional drug resistance. 4. Proper patient selection is critical for the success of shorter regimens. Patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB, who do not have resistance to fluoroquinolones, are expected to benefit the most. This strategy not only improves treatment outcomes but also helps prevent the development of resistance to key drugs like bedaquiline. 5. The implementation of shorter regimens should only occur in settings where routine drug susceptibility testing (DST) for rifampicin and fluoroquinolones is guaranteed. This ensures the regimen’s effectiveness and prevents the amplification of drug resistance. 6. Efforts must continue to expand access to DST for all relevant drugs, including newer medications. In the absence of specific DST for bedaquiline, resistance should be monitored through minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assessments. 7. Resistance to other anti-TB drugs should be monitored in accordance with WHO recommendations to ensure comprehensive management of drug-resistant TB. 8. Evidence suggests that regimens containing both bedaquiline and linezolid yield favorable outcomes. However, until further evidence is available, the inclusion of linezolid in shorter, all-oral regimens is not recommended outside of operational research settings. 9. A patient-centered approach is essential to ensure full adherence to treatment. This includes providing adequate support to patients throughout the treatment process. 10. The implementation of shorter regimens requires routine DST not only for patient selection but also for monitoring the emergence of resistance during treatment. 11. Active drug safety monitoring and management systems must be in place to detect, manage, and report adverse events or drug toxicities promptly. This ensures the safety of patients undergoing treatment. 12. Research priorities include studies comparing all-oral shorter regimens containing bedaquiline and linezolid, as well as exploring their effectiveness and safety in different subgroups, such as pregnant women and those with HIV. 13. Additional research is needed to understand the mechanisms of resistance acquisition to bedaquiline and to identify genetic markers for resistance. Efforts should also focus on standardizing data collection to contribute to global recommendations. 14. Tuberculosis remains a significant global public health threat, with MDR/RR-TB emerging as a major challenge due to poor management of both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant TB. 15. While MDR/RR-TB is treatable, it has traditionally required long treatment regimens with potentially toxic drugs. Recent advances in diagnostics and medications have improved detection and treatment success rates in some national programs. 16. Despite these improvements, global treatment success rates remain suboptimal, with only 56% success for MDR/RR-TB and 39% for extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) in 2016. 17. Shorter, all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimens of 9–12 months have shown promise in observational studies, offering better tolerability and reduced toxicity compared to longer regimens. 18. The balance of effects strongly favors the intervention of shorter regimens, as they are associated with fewer adverse events and a significant reduction in mortality compared to longer regimens with injectable agents. 19. Cost savings are anticipated with shorter regimens due to reduced hospitalization rates, fewer adverse events, and lower retreatment and loss-to-follow-up rates. 20. The overall certainty of evidence for the effects of shorter regimens is rated as very low, primarily due to reliance on observational data and potential residual confounding. However, the benefits of shorter regimens outweigh the risks when implemented with proper safeguards.
